h.title: Java backend developer who sees the whole system
h.sub: Oracle, Spring, automation and AI, from the database to deployment.
h.value: I build and evolve Java applications for the public sector, and I make the design calls from start to finish. Outside work I run my own homelab, so I also know what sits underneath the code.
h.ai: This site was built with AI agents.
a.p1: I'm a Java backend developer based in Barcelona. I've spent over {years} years at Inetum, from intern to Senior Software Developer, evolving public-sector applications with Java, Spring and Oracle. Day to day I make most of the architecture decisions on the features I own.
a.p2: My focus is getting systems to do on their own what used to be done by hand: tuning heavy queries, migrating complex PL/SQL logic to Java, and automating processes. I don't think a backend makes sense in isolation, so outside work I run a homelab, automate with n8n and build with AI agents. This site was made that way.
a.ltp: In the long run I'd like to move toward managing teams: I like working with people and helping others grow.
p.lead: One thread across three areas: understanding the whole system, not just my layer.
p.b.1: Heavy Oracle queries tuned. Typical examples: ~30 s down to ~5 s, or ~1 min down to ~10 s; smaller ones from ~10 s to ≤1 s.
p.b.2: Complex PL/SQL logic migrated to Java so it's easier to maintain.
p.b.3: Data from other public bodies integrated into our own applications.
p.b.4: REST and SOAP integrations; hands-on work with legacy systems.
p.b.5: Oracle Certified Associate, Java SE 8 Programmer (Mar 2026).
p.s.1: A Proxmox homelab: one VM for Docker, LXCs for networking and services, Nginx Proxy Manager and AdGuard Home.
p.s.2: Services published through Cloudflare Tunnel from behind CG-NAT, with no open ports.
p.s.3: Cloudflare Access with 2FA in front of what's exposed, fail2ban, a LAN-only Proxmox firewall, and sensitive services kept on the local network.
p.s.4: Native Proxmox backups with a defined policy (daily, keep last 3).
p.s.5: I host third-party services, such as openGym, a gym tracker with passkey login.
p.i.1: Automated processes at work: periodic extracts now produced by a job and sent to the user by Excel or email; weekly checks on manual changes; processes that used to need a manual step and no longer do.
p.i.2: My own n8n instance, with a daily Telegram digest (weather, news, tasks, markets and updates from my apps).
p.i.3: Homelab task management through Claude Code and a Vikunja MCP.
p.i.4: Development with AI agents. Claude Code 101 course completed (Anthropic, Apr 2026).
p.i.5: At work, early steps with AI: system prompts for agents, including an incident-handling agent built with Copilot.
e.co: Public-sector projects. From intern to Senior, over {years} years on the job.
e.s.1: I run feature work end to end, mostly on my own, and decide the architecture: whether something should be a job, a manual service, or something else.
e.s.2: I integrate data from other public bodies into our applications.
e.s.3: I automate processes so users no longer have to act manually.
e.s.4: I resolve complex production incidents and help teammates, including onboarding new people to the project.
e.d.1: High-cost Oracle queries cut to half their time or less, often to a quarter.
e.d.2: Jobs replacing recurring manual tasks: extracts, reports and checks.
e.d.3: Logic migrated from PL/SQL to Java.
e.d.5: Integration with REST and SOAP services.
e.i.1: Support on enhancements and bug fixes in internal web applications.
e.i.2: First contact with the Java, Spring, ExtJS and Oracle stack, and with Scrum.
e.i.3: Training in Angular, Ionic and NestJS (training only, not my working stack).
pr.tag: A custom dashboard for my homelab.
pr.p: I was using Homepage, but it can't combine data across apps (for example, a single timeline of outages, n8n run failures and Proxmox events) and doesn't integrate with n8n. I also wanted a start page with links and search.
pr.d1: FastAPI with server-rendered pages and htmx. No SPA, no JS build step: few dependencies and readable code.
pr.d2: In its own LXC, not as a Docker stack. A dashboard that reports on the infrastructure shouldn't go down with the thing it watches.
pr.d3: Auto-update: a systemd timer checks main every 5 minutes and, if there are changes, pulls and restarts. Outbound requests only: no inbound ports, no runner.
pr.d4: Reachable from the local network only, since it gathers a lot of sensitive information.
pr.d5: The update service runs as root because it has to restart the app. I accepted it and documented it, on a single-purpose LXC, rather than add sudoers rules.
pr.r1: Running in production on my network, with tests that run without external services (each integration falls back to “not configured”) and CI on every PR. It replaced Homepage. Today it shows the state of each integration on one screen; combining data across them (the single timeline) is still a pending goal.
pr.r2: Rollback is simple: git + systemd, plus a Proxmox snapshot before big changes.
pr.lt: I started without a detailed design and discovered requirements along the way, so some parts came out worse than I wanted. I'd plan up front today. This site starts from exactly that lesson.
hm.lead: A home server on Proxmox, behind CG-NAT, and the decisions behind it.
hm.ctx: A single physical server (no RAID, no hardware redundancy). Proxmox VE as hypervisor for VMs, LXC, snapshots and native backups, and room to experiment without breaking the base. A Debian VM running Docker for applications; LXCs for the tunnel, DNS and other network services.
hm.decp: Each one as problem, decision and why.
g.dw: Left-to-right flow diagram. Internet reaches a Cloudflare Tunnel, which runs from an LXC inside a single Proxmox server, to Nginx Proxy Manager, which routes traffic to the Docker stacks of a VM (n8n, Vikunja, openGym and a website), managed with Portainer. A second path, Tailscale, gives VPN access to the local network through a subnet-router LXC. Next to it are an LXC with AdGuard Home and another with the homepanel dashboard, local network only. Outside the server, a repurposed Android phone checks that the server responds. No inbound ports are open and the server is behind CG-NAT.
g.dt: Top-to-bottom flow diagram. Internet reaches a Cloudflare Tunnel, which runs from an LXC inside a single Proxmox server, to Nginx Proxy Manager, which routes traffic to the Docker stacks of a VM (n8n, Vikunja, openGym and a website), managed with Portainer. A second path, Tailscale, gives VPN access to the local network through a subnet-router LXC. Inside the server there is also an LXC with AdGuard Home and another with the homepanel dashboard, local network only. Outside the server, a repurposed Android phone checks that the server responds. No inbound ports are open and the server is behind CG-NAT.

g.t.net: visitors and my devices away from home
d1.p: I'm behind CG-NAT and can't open ports.
d1.d: Cloudflare Tunnel from a dedicated LXC.
d1.w: The connection is outbound only, so no public IP is needed.
d2.d: Tailscale, with a subnet router in an LXC.
d2.w: WireGuard needs an inbound port, and Cloudflare WARP would fail during LaLiga's blocks on Cloudflare ranges.
d2.l: If the server goes down, the VPN goes with it.
d3.p: A monitor running on the server can't tell you the server is down.
d3.d: Use a repurposed Android phone as an independent monitoring node (work in progress).
d3.w: It has to live on separate hardware; same reasoning as homepanel's dedicated LXC.
d4.t: Docker in a VM, not an LXC
d4.w: To avoid nested Docker inside unprivileged containers, given my experience at the time (comfortable with Linux, still learning Docker and networking).
d5.p: I wanted my own mail server.
d5.w: Behind CG-NAT I can't receive mail, and a residential IP has no sending reputation. A VPS relay would be the only viable route.
d6.d: Native Proxmox backups, no Proxmox Backup Server.
d6.w: It would be overkill for a single node. Policy: daily, keep last 3.
d7.t: My own network for the homelab
d7.p: The homelab and my machines shared the ISP's network, and the start was chaotic.
d7.d: My own router for the homelab and my machines, separate from the ISP router.
d7.w: I control the network I work on, and it's kept apart from the home Wi-Fi.
s.p: Some days access to my services timed out without any error. It turned out to be ISP blocks on Cloudflare IP ranges during football matches, which hit everything behind Cloudflare. There's no fix on my side; the lesson was to check the match calendar before debugging the network.
